explanations.answer: A very large assembly of Israelites
explanations.explanation: Ezra the priest is facedown before the house of God, and a very large assembly of Israelites gathers around him. The text says men, women and children (Ezra 10:1). One man on the ground praying, and then the whole neighborhood shows up. I think that's a lot of people to find standing over you when you lift your head.

Not just the leading priests, friend. The text says a very large assembly of Israelites gathered around Ezra the priest. That means men, women and children (Ezra 10:1). That's a crowd, not a staff meeting.

Small is the one word that doesn't fit here. Ezra the priest is praying when a very large assembly of Israelites gathers around him (Ezra 10:1). The text says men, women and children, so Levites aren't the only ones standing there. If I tried to bake for that crowd, I'd run out of dough before the second row.

True. Ezra is praying and confessing, weeping and facedown, and the text says the people wept bitterly as well (Ezra 10:1). The crowd isn't standing around watching. They're crying right along with him.

It's actually true. The text says Ezra prayed and confessed, weeping and falling facedown, and the people wept bitterly as well (Ezra 10:1). So the crowd that gathers around him isn't quiet. They're weeping right along with him.

Hope is the word. Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, says it right after admitting the unfaithfulness: “…yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel.” (Ezra 10:2). He says the hard part out loud and still says there's hope. That's a man who looks at a burnt batch and says the oven still works.

Danger isn't the word, friend. Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, admits they've been unfaithful, then says, “…yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel.” (Ezra 10:2). He's looking for a way forward, not just naming a problem. Hope is what he lands on.

Shame is a fair guess after hearing that confession, but it's not the word he picks. Shecaniah son of Jehiel, an Elamite, says they've been unfaithful, and then says, “…yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel.” (Ezra 10:2). He names the problem honestly, then he points to hope. That's the turn in his sentence.

explanations.answer: Send away the foreign wives and their children
explanations.explanation: Shecaniah says, “So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children…” (Ezra 10:3). He adds, “Let it be done according to the Law.” I think this is a heavy moment, because real families are in it. It's a serious covenant, made before God.

explanations.answer: Rebuild the walls all around Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: Walls aren't part of this covenant, friend. Shecaniah wants a covenant before God to send away all the foreign wives and their children (Ezra 10:3). The matter on the table is the people's unfaithfulness, not construction. Nobody in this scene is grabbing a trowel.

explanations.answer: Keep a fast for forty days and nights
explanations.explanation: No fast is in this covenant. Shecaniah asks the people to make a covenant before God to send away all the foreign wives and their children (Ezra 10:3). Ezra does go without food and water, but that comes later and it's his own mourning (Ezra 10:6). The covenant itself is about the wives and children.

That's what Shecaniah promises. He says, “Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (Ezra 10:4). Ezra is handed the job and told he won't carry it alone. That's a good thing to hear when the load is this heavy.

explanations.answer: The people will pick a new leader
explanations.explanation: Nobody's swapping leaders here. Shecaniah tells Ezra, “…this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you.” (Ezra 10:4). The responsibility stays with Ezra, and the people promise to stand behind him. It's backup, not a replacement.

explanations.answer: The people will return to Babylon
explanations.explanation: Babylon isn't mentioned in this promise. Shecaniah says, “…we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (Ezra 10:4). That's a promise to stay and stand with Ezra. Nobody is packing a bag.

Swear is the word. Ezra gets up and makes the leading priests, Levites and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said, and they took the oath (Ezra 10:5). An oath is a serious promise made before God, not a casual nod. They don't mumble through it either, because the text says they took it.

No ballots here, friend. Ezra makes the leading priests, Levites and all Israel take an oath, and they took the oath (Ezra 10:5). An oath is a promise sworn, not a show of hands. Nobody is counting a tally.

Waiting is the opposite of what happens. Ezra gets up and makes the leading priests, Levites and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said (Ezra 10:5). Then the text says they took the oath. No one is told to hold off.

It's the other way around. The text says that while Ezra stayed in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib, he ate no food and drank no water (Ezra 10:6). The reason it gives is that he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. So there's no meal with the leaders at all.

That's right. While Ezra stays in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib, he eats no food and drinks no water (Ezra 10:6). The text says he's mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. No meal, no table, just mourning.

Three days is what they get. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). That's a short window to get to Jerusalem. I'd have been packing the minute the announcement ended.

Seven would be a full week, and they don't get that. The text says whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property (Ezra 10:8). Three days is a tight window. Even a week would feel short for a trip.

Forty days would be a long road, but the text gives much less. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property (Ezra 10:8). Three days, and then the consequences. That's not a window for a long trip.

explanations.answer: He loses his property and is expelled from the assembly
explanations.explanation: That's the consequence. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). The text says this was according to the counsel of the leaders and elders. It's a serious deadline, which is why everybody makes it.

explanations.answer: He pays a fine in silver to the house of God
explanations.explanation: Silver isn't mentioned here. The text says whoever didn't appear would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). That means losing everything he owned, not paying a fine. The leaders and elders gave this counsel.

explanations.answer: He is sent back to Babylon to live for good
explanations.explanation: No trip to Babylon is mentioned. The text says whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). Expelled from the assembly is the line to hold onto. And losing the property was part of it.

The heavy rain. On the twentieth day of the ninth month, the people sit in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). So they're nervous about the matter and soaked at the same time. I think that's a rough combination for a long sit.

The text doesn't mention any wind. It says the people sat in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). The weather in this scene is rain. It's a wet day to be sitting outside.

No locusts here, friend. The people sit in the square at the house of God trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). The weather is rain, and plenty of it. It's an uncomfortable day without any insects.

Separate is the word. Ezra the priest says, “Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” (Ezra 10:11). Confession comes first, then doing God's will. I think this is a heavy thing to say to a crowd, and he says it plainly.

Defend isn't the word he uses. Ezra the priest says, “Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” (Ezra 10:11). He first tells them to make a confession to the LORD and do His will. Nothing in the sentence asks them to guard anything.

The people have already gathered, so Ezra doesn't ask for that. They're sitting in the square when Ezra the priest says, “Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives.” (Ezra 10:11). Gathering was the job of the earlier proclamation. His word here is separate.

explanations.answer: Many people and the rainy season
explanations.explanation: That's what they say. The assembly answers, “But there are many people here, and it is the rainy season. We are not able to stay out in the open.” (Ezra 10:13). They also say it isn't the work of one or two days. So they agree with Ezra, they just need a plan that works for the weather and the crowd.

explanations.answer: Too few priests to help out
explanations.explanation: Priests aren't the problem they raise. The assembly says, “…there are many people here, and it is the rainy season.” (Ezra 10:13). They also say it isn't the work of one or two days, because they have transgressed greatly in this matter. The trouble is crowd size and weather, not helpers.

No enemies come up here. The assembly says, “…there are many people here, and it is the rainy season. We are not able to stay out in the open.” (Ezra 10:13). Those are the two things they name. The crowd is big and the rain is heavy.

explanations.answer: Leaders represent everyone while towns come at set times
explanations.explanation: That's the plan. The assembly says, “Let our leaders represent the whole assembly. Then let everyone in our towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time…” (Ezra 10:14). So the crowd doesn't have to stand out in the rain. It's a way to handle a big job without everyone being there at once.

explanations.answer: Each family handles its own case quietly at home
explanations.explanation: Nothing is handled quietly at home. The assembly proposes that their leaders represent the whole assembly, and that everyone in their towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time (Ezra 10:14). The elders and judges of each town come along too. It's an open process, not a private one.

explanations.answer: Everyone gathers again once the rainy season ends
explanations.explanation: They don't wait for the rain to end. The assembly says, “Let our leaders represent the whole assembly.” Then each town's men come at an appointed time with the elders and judges of that town (Ezra 10:14). So the work spreads out instead of waiting.

Judges is right. The men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). So each town sends its own elders and judges along with the men concerned. That's a town-by-town setup, with people who know the local folks.

Singers aren't in this plan. The men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). Judges are the ones named alongside the elders. Singers do show up later in the passage, but only in the list (Ezra 10:24).

No soldiers are named. The assembly says each town's men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). Judges are the ones sitting beside the elders. It's a setup for deciding matters, not for fighting.

explanations.answer: The fierce anger of their God
explanations.explanation: That's what they name. The plan goes on “…until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (Ezra 10:14). They say it themselves, and they say it as a group. I think that's a sober thing to hear from a crowd sitting in the rain.

explanations.answer: The armies of the nearby peoples
explanations.explanation: No armies in this line. The assembly says the plan continues “…until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (Ezra 10:14). The thing they want turned away is God's fierce anger. It's about the matter before God, not about a military threat.

explanations.answer: The heavy rain of the season
explanations.explanation: The rain is real, but it's not what they want turned away. They say the plan goes on “…until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (Ezra 10:14). They had just mentioned the rainy season as the reason for the plan (Ezra 10:13). The thing that matters most to them is God's anger.

Family heads is right. Ezra the priest selects men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families (Ezra 10:16). So the people picked are leaders in their own households. It's a good way to get a big job done.

Not singers, friend. The text says Ezra the priest selected men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families (Ezra 10:16). Singers appear later in the list of men, but they aren't the ones chosen here (Ezra 10:24). These men speak for their families.

No guards are mentioned. Ezra the priest selects men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families (Ezra 10:16). Each one speaks for his own family. That's a different job than standing watch.

They finish the whole job. The text says that by the first day of the first month they had dealt with all the men who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:17). They started on the first day of the tenth month (Ezra 10:16). So it wasn't half, it was every man.

That's right. The text says that by the first day of the first month they had dealt with all the men who had married foreign women (Ezra 10:17). They began on the first day of the tenth month (Ezra 10:16). So they went through every case, not half.
